title: Breathing: what to do and when
summary: Slow breathing calms the body, but timing matters. What you can try on training days, before the stand, at the call and after a miss.

body.html: When you are stressed, your body reacts on its own: the heart beats faster and breathing gets shallow. Breathing is one of the few parts of this you can control directly. Many studies show that slow breathing, at about 6 breaths a minute, calms the body: the heartbeat settles into a calmer, more flexible rhythm (researchers measure this as heart rate variability).

Whether it raises your score is much less clear. Small studies with sport shooters and one study with police pistol shooters found it helped, but we found no study in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting.

html: Training days: 5–10 minutes of slow breathing at about 6 breaths a minute, for example in for 4 seconds and out for 6.
2–5 minutes before the stand: 6–10 slow breaths, with a longer breath out if that feels comfortable.
In the routine, just before the call: one natural breath out and loose shoulders, then the call.
After a lost target: one slow breath out as the signal to reset.

body.html: If you practise slow breathing on ordinary days, your body learns to calm down faster, so on competition day it may come more easily. A heart-rate sensor that shows your heart rhythm live (this is called biofeedback) can help, but you do not need one.

Before the stand there is no time pressure, so a few slow breaths can lower tension without getting in the way. In Compak® Sporting, if your squad has six shooters, the wait behind station 1 is a good moment (Chapter 17 · Squad rotation through the stations).

Just before the call, keep the breath short and natural. In one lab study, slow paced breathing slowed reaction time. Clay shooting starts with a reaction to the target, and the delay after the call is often hard to predict (in Sporting™, and in Compak® Sporting with a manual release). So one easy breath out is enough here.
After a miss, one slow breath out can mark the end of that target. It works as a reset signal: see Reset after a miss.

You may hear of box breathing: in, hold, out and hold, four counts each. It is one option you can try. When researchers compared it with other ways of breathing, it did no better; in one study, simply breathing out longer than you breathe in worked better.
The “physiological sigh” is two breaths in through the nose and one long breath out. In one study, five minutes a day of it improved mood. We found no study of it just before a shot.
Many people find a breath out that is longer than the breath in relaxing. Studies disagree on whether it adds anything, so choose the rhythm that feels comfortable.
Breathing exercises should feel easy. If you feel dizzy or short of breath, return to normal breathing. If you have a heart or lung condition, ask your doctor first.

notes.html: Teach slow breathing away from the stand, on training days. On the stand, keep only the short natural breath out before the call.

key_points.html: Slow breathing calms the body; you can practise it 5–10 minutes on training days.
Before the stand: a few slow breaths, with a comfortable longer breath out.
At the call: one natural breath out and loose shoulders, not long slow breathing.
After a miss: one slow breath out to start the reset.
Box breathing and the physiological sigh are options to try; research on them is limited.

did_you_know.html: Slow breathing at about 6 breaths a minute is sometimes called resonance breathing: at this pace, heart rate and breathing tend to rise and fall together.

quiz.q: What can you try just before the call?

options.text: Ten slow breaths at six a minute
One natural breath out, shoulders down
Holding your breath for a count of four

quiz.explain: Long, slow breathing right before the call may slow your reaction; keep slow breaths for before the stand.

quiz.q: What does research say about box breathing?

options.text: It works clearly better than other methods
It is not allowed in competitions
It is one option, with little research

quiz.explain: When researchers compared box breathing with other ways of breathing, it was not better; you can try it, but it is not a sure fix.

quiz.q: When is slow breathing at about six breaths a minute a good fit?

options.text: On training days and before the stand
Right up to the very moment of the call
Only after the whole round is over

quiz.explain: Use slow breathing when there is no time pressure; at the call, one natural breath out is enough.
